We did not invent him out of an idea. Ignatius wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and he put it as hard as it can be put: close your ears, he said, when anyone tells you something that goes against Jesus Christ, who was truly born of Mary, from the line of David, who truly ate and drank, who was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate, truly crucified and died. Not in appearance only, the way those he wrote against claimed. And he said Jesus was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. More than one of our own households uses those words, not only Ignatius's own. Ignatius calls him Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out.

That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks. None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone.

We cannot promise you a sudden certainty, because it was not sudden for the one among us who wrote about it. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words left him with, in his own phrase, a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. The voice of an ordinary person standing where you stand, struggling the way you are struggling - that voice is not in our record. Everyone whose words survive was already someone who could read and write, already someone near the center of things. We would rather tell you that plainly than pretend we have an answer we do not actually have.

What we can tell you is what we asked of someone who came to us: not certainty first, but a willingness to be taught. The teaching came before the water - the Two Ways, a way of life and a way of death, laid open as a real choice. After the teaching, then the water. The struggle you name may be exactly what that waiting was meant to hold.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. And we called Jesus Christ our God again and again - Ignatius does this in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out.

How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. The Spirit is named in our baptism: we baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But what the Spirit is in relation to the Father and the Son, we did not settle.

We can tell you plainly that we called Jesus God. We can tell you we baptized into a threefold name. We cannot tell you we had worked out how they fit together. If you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one overseer - the episkopos - or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. That is the foundation we held together, and it was never in question among us. One of us, Justin, went further and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. 

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight. Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement. It was not about what God is.

We can tell you this much more: God for us was the one who raised Jesus, and the one who would raise us the same way. We gave thanks to him over the cup and the bread. We called him Father. But we left no systematic account of his nature - no treatise working out how to speak rightly of what cannot be fully spoken. We held him, and we worshiped him, and we left the arguing to who should lead that worship.

We never settled doctrine the way you are asking. No council met to vote on what was true. No final judge stood above the argument. What we had instead was letters - letters carried between churches, copied, read aloud, argued over. When one church thought another had strayed, it wrote. Rome wrote to Corinth about removed elders. Ignatius wrote from under guard to several churches at once, pressing hard against people who said the Lord's flesh was only appearance. But those letters were persuasion, not rulings. No mechanism existed to enforce them if a church simply disagreed and kept going its own way.

The one thing we held to across distance was what had been handed down from the apostles. The apostles had appointed others after them to carry the teaching forward. But even that was an argument we made, not a settled structure we lived inside. Who counted as rightly appointed, and whether a teaching was genuinely apostolic or a later invention - those were the live questions, not the answers.

We should say plainly: the single-bishop pattern and the claim of unbroken succession from the apostles did eventually win. But they won afterward, not among us. In our own time they were still being argued for, not assumed.

The road to life begins with loving God and your neighbor, and not doing to another what you would not want done to you. That teaching assumes a person can walk one way or the other - it is a choice kept daily, not a condition settled before you were born. 

Whether a newborn child already carries guilt from Adam, or whether guilt begins only with your own choices - that question was not one we argued about in our own letters. What we can tell you is this: we taught the water - the baptisma - to people who had been taught first, who had fasted, and who walked to it themselves. We have no surviving instruction about infants at all. Whether that means we did not baptize them, or simply that no one wrote it down, we cannot say. The silence is real, and we will not fill it.

We will answer what we actually did, where we actually did it.

In at least some of our households, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud. They read the writings of the prophets, and where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left. This goes on for as long as there is time. Then whoever leads us explains what has been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves receives it - the same way everyone in the room does, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

Most of us could not read. Reading, for us, was not a private thing done alone with a scroll. It was done out loud, in the assembly - the ekklesia - with the whole community present to hear it together. The explanation came right there, in the same gathering, from the one trusted to lead.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. One of us, Justin, reads the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. That is the purpose he names: not simply to know what was written, but to see how it had already been speaking of the one we now followed.

We should say plainly, too: we were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. A fixed boundary around what counted as scripture - that belongs to a world that came after ours.

We cannot tell you what you are missing, because we cannot know what you are looking for. What we can tell you is what the scriptures were for us, and what kind of reading that was.

We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. When we gathered on the day of the sun, someone read aloud - the writings of the prophets, and where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left. This went on for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it: the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. One of us, Justin, reads the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. He argued that Moses wrote long before Plato, and that Plato himself had drawn on Moses's own account of creation. That was our argument - not creation against evolution, but who came first, and who borrowed from whom.

We should say this plainly, too: where something in the older writings troubled a reader, none of us wrote down feeling that trouble ourselves. But we can tell you the trouble you feel was not invented by you. It was real enough in our own time that someone near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of those older writings harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account tells you the trouble you feel was not invented by you.

We never settled it. That is the first honest thing we have to tell you. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

What we did agree on was the ground itself. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. That chain mattered to us - not as a list of names, but as the living claim that what we taught and how we gathered went back to those who walked with him. We read what the apostles wrote alongside the apostolic testimony still handed on among us, with no fixed boundary yet between them. That was the inheritance we received. The fight was over who carried it forward now.

Rome is the clearest case we can show you. In Rome, a council of elders held the governing together - episkopos and presbyteros used for the same people, interchangeably, with no single bishop standing above them. That college led, taught, and wrote on behalf of the whole church there. A single bishop's office came later, near the end of our own years or just after them. When Rome wrote to Corinth - a long, unrequested letter about elders wrongly removed from office - it was that council speaking, not one man.

We cannot give you ordinary voices on any of this. Every word that survives was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The people who simply belonged, who came to the table and listened as the letters were read aloud - they are not the ones you are hearing from.

There was one other kind of authority among us, harder to pin down: the prophet, the one who spoke as the Spirit prompted. Welcomed where genuine, tested where doubtful. In some places the settled offices of overseer and elder were taking the prophet's place. That replacement was happening during our own years, not after them. It tells you how unsettled the whole question still was.

We will not claim a clean record. Here is the clearest case of real conflict we have. A church in Corinth removed some of its own presbyters from office. Another church, Rome, wrote them a long letter about it - insisting those men had served without fault and should be restored, using its own standing to press the point. But the letter we have is Rome's, not Corinth's. We don't have Corinth's own reasons for what it did. We don't have the removed men's own words either. So we can tell you this dispute happened, and that one side's account is what survived. We cannot tell you, honestly, who was right, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

There is something else we have to tell you plainly. Most of us could not read. Most of us left no letters because we could not have written one. Everything we left behind was written by the few among us who could write - and it is a city record. What an ordinary believer made of the teaching as it was read aloud, what faith sounded like in a village rather than a city street, how the gospel traveled where no letters went - our own words cannot show you. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page. So when we failed someone who had no voice to begin with, we cannot even tell you it happened.

Before anything else, you were taught. The teaching of the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life begins with loving God who made you, and loving your neighbor as yourself. Then comes the rule: whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else. It went down into the texture of ordinary dealings - do not be quick to anger, do not hold a grudge, share what you have rather than calling it your own. This was not a moment's instruction; it was the ground you walked on before the water.

Then came the baptisma - the washing that marks entry into the community. It was given after the teaching and after fasting. Running water, if you could find it - still water if not, or water poured three times over your head, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. You fasted beforehand - a day or two - and the person baptizing you fasted right beside you. Only after the water could you come to the table.

After that, you gathered with us. On the day we gathered - in Rome, the day named for the sun - someone read aloud. We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traces it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues. Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

Here is what we can show you as direct connection. Rome, writing to Corinth, says it this way: the apostles preached the Gospel to us from the Lord Jesus Christ; Jesus Christ was sent from God. The apostles appointed the first converts to be overseers and deacons of those who would believe. That letter itself dates to our own time - it is not a later claim about us, but our own voice speaking. The inheritance itself is real: this world received, rather than invented, the conviction that legitimate teaching and practice must trace to apostolic testimony. Scripture read alongside living apostolic testimony, not against a closed canon - an inheritance received from the apostolic generation directly.

What we cannot give you is an unbroken chain of names and dates proving every detail survived unchanged. The water, the shared meal, the two ways taught before baptism - we hold them as apostolic. We cannot produce a signed register from the apostles' own hands saying they did it exactly this way first.

We were told plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. That was taught to one of us, Hermas, and it names doubting for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. The table itself stood the same way in both: it formed us into one body, again and again.

We cannot give you one day that stands for everyone. A member's ordinary day looked entirely different depending on which of our two answers to 'who leads' their community held. And we need to say plainly: most of us could not read or write, so the people who actually filled our rooms left no account in their own words. Everything we can tell you was written by the few among us who could write - and it is a city record: Antioch, the towns of Asia Minor, Rome. What an ordinary believer made of the teaching as it was read aloud, what faith sounded like in a village rather than a city street, how the gospel traveled where no letters went - our own words cannot show you. When we tell you what we taught and how we gathered, know that you are hearing our writers, and our cities. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page.

What we can tell you is the shape of a gathering day. On the day called Sunday, everyone who lives in the cities or in the country gathers together in one place. Someone reads aloud - the memoirs the apostles left, and the words of the prophets before them, for as long as there is time. Then whoever leads us explains what has been read. After that we pray together, standing. Then comes the thanksgiving - the eucharistia, our word for the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. Those who serve - the diakonoi, who carry help to the widow, the prisoner, and the stranger who cannot repay - bring what has been blessed out to those who could not come.

Before any of that, before the water itself - the baptisma, the washing that marks entry - we were taught the Two Ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. What an ordinary Tuesday looked like between one gathering and the next - that is exactly what our writers did not write down.

We can give you some of what was asked, not everything. Before the water - the baptisma - someone was taught the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death, and they are very different. What the teaching asked of anyone, it asked of everyone - no idols, no murder, no adultery, no stealing, no coveting what belongs to another. And it went further than that: do not even desire what you would not want done to you; share what you have instead of calling it your own. That last part is plain enough: the teaching pressed toward a real giving up of what was yours alone.

How far that reached in practice, we cannot say with one voice. In Justin's own account of how we gather on the day named for the sun, those who have means bring what they can, and it is distributed to orphans, widows, prisoners, and anyone in need. That is real, but it is not the same as no longer owning anything. Some of our own communities met in houses large enough to hold us - someone owned those houses, or was trusted to use them. So the picture is uneven: a teaching that said share what you have, and a practice where sharing happened every time we gathered, but not a rule that no one could own anything at all.

For the women among us, there was a cost we cannot measure. Women were taught, greeted by name in our letters, and remembered as leaders of households where we gathered. But not a single sentence any woman of ours wrote or spoke, in her own words, survives. What it cost them to belong and to serve, and whether the teaching asked more of them than it asked of men, our record cannot show you. That silence is real, and we will not fill it.

Marriage was treated as belonging to the whole household, not sealed off from it.

We would rather tell you the truth than a comfortable answer. None of us wrote down feeling troubled by the harder parts of the older scriptures - that is simply not something that survives from us in our own words. But we can tell you this: one teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of those older writings harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account tells you the trouble you feel was not invented by you. It was real enough in our own time that someone built a whole rejection out of it - at least as his enemies tell it.

Here is what unsettled us in a different way, one we argued about openly: who should lead, and whether one overseer or a council of elders held us together. The episkopos - the one who watches over a community's table and its unity - stood at the center of some of our households. In others, a council of elders led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. A member's ordinary day looked entirely different depending on which answer their own household held. We never settled it. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs.

The governor's account is genuinely useful to us - and we will tell you plainly why its origin under torture matters, and where it cannot be trusted.

What he wrote down is the only outside description of our gathering we have from our own years. It names the day, the hour before dawn, the hymn to Christ as God, and the oath we swore - not to steal, not to break faith, not to commit adultery. Then a second meeting, for a meal his informants called common yet harmless. All of that matches what our own letters say about how we gathered. Where it agrees with what we ourselves wrote, the agreement is real.

But we have to name two limits just as plainly. First: he did not see any of it himself. He wrote down what people told him, and some of what he learned came from two enslaved women he had tortured to get it - ministrae, his own word for them, not ours. What they said under those conditions, whether it was the whole truth or only what would make the pain stop, we cannot know. Second: we have no record at all of what those two women would have said in their own words, without a torturer standing over them. Everything we know of them passed through his hands.

So the account is useful where it lines up with what we already know we did. It cannot be trusted to tell you what those two women actually thought, or whether there was anything they kept back to protect the rest of us. We would rather say that plainly than pretend torture produces reliable testimony.

We cannot tell you how any one household among us would have met you at the door. Nothing in our own record answers that directly. What we can give you is the pattern we held up before every person who came to us.

Before the water, we taught the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. That teaching was laid open before everyone - it asked the same thing of whoever heard it. Then came baptism - the baptisma, the washing that marks entry. After that, you could come to the table. That was the shape of belonging for us.

On the day we gathered, someone read aloud - the writings of the prophets, and where a community had them, what the apostles had written. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. After that came the thanksgiving - the eucharistia, the meal of bread and cup. The same bread, the same cup, was set before whoever had walked the road to it.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. What we asked people to turn from, we asked them to turn from. What we called them toward, we called everyone toward. It is not our place to judge what you are. We can only tell you honestly what we held, and let you weigh what it means for you.

We will give you both of our own answers, because we actually held both. One of us, Justin, argued that anyone who lived reasonably - Socrates among the Greeks, others among peoples you might not expect him to name - was, in a real sense, already a Christian, born before Christ or not. He wrote plainly: those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though people have thought them atheists. That is about as far from 'you're all going to hell' as anything we wrote. And yet in at least one of our own communities, the way a new member was taught was stark: two roads, a way of life and a way of death, nothing in between named. We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community. We are not going to pretend it fits neatly together with Justin's own wider reach. They are both truly ours.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not the fate of outsiders. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight. The question you are asking - we held it both ways at once, and never settled it.
